strengths: The paper addresses a clearly articulated and practically important problem: existing PDE-constrained diffusion methods enforce constraints on the posterior mean E[x0|xt], incurring the Jensen's Gap. The motivation is well-supported by both a synthetic analytical example (MoG with tractable score, Fig. 2a-c) and a training-time demonstration (Fig. 2d), which strengthens the problem statement beyond mere assertion.

The proposed solution is simple and well-aligned with the diagnosis: enforcing PDE residuals on the final output of a distilled student directly matches the sample-level constraint objective, sidestepping the posterior-mean surrogate entirely. This decoupling of physics enforcement from the diffusion trajectory is a clean conceptual contribution.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: three main PDE benchmarks plus six additional ones (Appendix E), four metrics including distributional measures (MMSE, SMSE, FPD), forward/inverse/reconstruction downstream tasks, a compute-matched comparison (Table 3), and component-attribution ablations (Table 6) that honestly show distillation alone gives speed while final-sample PDE supervision drives the physical-consistency gain. The architecture-robustness (Table 9), diversity (Table 7), teacher-quality sensitivity (Table 8), and dynamic-weighting (Table 10) experiments demonstrate careful robustness analysis.

The theoretical appendix (B.3) provides a supporting linear-Gaussian analysis showing why score learning in constrained directions is slow (Theorem B.1) and why the distillation penalty shrinks constraint violation (Theorem B.2). While restricted to toy settings, the paper appropriately frames distributional fidelity claims as empirical rather than overclaiming theoretical guarantees.

The limitations section is honest (dependence on teacher quality, need for a reliable residual operator, residual hyperparameter tuning), and the supplementary review-driven ablations (Appendix G) show responsiveness to previously raised concerns.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core recipe is a fairly standard one-step distillation (rectified flow / DMD / consistency model components are adopted from prior work) with an added penalty term on the student output. The novelty lies mainly in the placement of the constraint and the empirical demonstration, which reviewers may view as an engineering-level combination rather than a fundamentally new method.

Baselines are reimplemented in the authors' own codebase (Appendix D.4) rather than run from official code, and some hyperparameters (e.g., DiffusionPDE's guidance weight set equal to lambda_train) may not reflect tuned baseline configurations. This weakens the certainty of the claimed margins over PIDM, DiffusionPDE, and ECI, especially since reported baseline numbers differ from those in original publications.

The strongest headline results come from PIDDM-ref, which uses inference-time latent optimization on top of the distilled student; the teacher baseline does not receive an equivalent refinement budget in Table 1, so comparisons against the Teacher row (e.g., PIDDM-ref beating the teacher on MMSE/SMSE/FPD) conflate the method's distillation contribution with the extra optimization stage. The compute-matched Table 3 partially mitigates this but only covers one dataset.

Theoretical analysis is limited to linear score networks, Gaussian targets, and a single hard constraint direction; no analysis connects the method's behavior to realistic nonlinear PDE residual landscapes, where the residual penalty could bias samples toward a measure-zero constraint manifold and distort the learned distribution. The diversity analysis (Table 7) is only on Darcy.

Main result tables (1, 2, 5) lack error bars or standard deviations across seeds; only a small variance study (Table 12) is provided. Given that several margins between PIDDM-1 and strong baselines (e.g., ECI on MMSE for Darcy) are modest, statistical robustness is not fully established.

Scalability is untested: all experiments use small FNO teachers on grids up to 128x128 or 1D problems with near-analytical PDE residuals. It remains unclear whether the framework extends to harder, high-dimensional, or chaotic systems (e.g., 3D turbulence, multi-physics) where residual operators are expensive or stiff, which limits claims of broad practical significance.

strengths: The core observation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: enforcing PDE constraints on the posterior mean E[x0|xt] during training/sampling introduces a Jensen's Gap relative to constraints on the final sample x0, and the paper provides both synthetic demonstrations (Fig. 2) and a training-time manifestation (Fig. 2d) of this issue.

The proposed fix is simple and practical: post-hoc distillation of the teacher diffusion model into a one-step student with the PDE residual applied directly to the student's final output, which sidesteps the posterior-mean surrogate entirely and yields a large efficiency win (1 NFE vs. hundreds for baselines).

Broad empirical evaluation: three main PDE benchmarks in the main text plus six additional benchmarks (Table 5), downstream forward/inverse/reconstruction tasks (Table 2), a compute-matched comparison (Table 3), and extensive ablations (Fig. 3, Tables 4, 6-13) covering distillation backbones, teacher quality, architectures, hard-constraint masking, and diversity preservation.

The paper is honest about the status of its claims (e.g., 'distributional fidelity claims remain empirical rather than an end-to-end theoretical guarantee') and includes a clear limitations section acknowledging teacher dependence and hyperparameter sensitivity.

Appendix B.3 offers a simplified analytical treatment (linear-Gaussian target, diagonal student) giving intuition for why final-sample supervision can suppress constraint violations where score-space guidance struggles.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the method is a fairly straightforward combination of known components - vanilla knowledge/rectified-flow/DMD/consistency-model distillation plus a PDE penalty on the final output. Final-sample physics enforcement already exists in noise-prompting methods (D-Flow, InitNo) and hard-projection approaches (ECI); the contribution is primarily an engineering repackaging (distillation + final-sample penalty) rather than a new conceptual insight.

Theoretical support is thin relative to the central claim. Theorem B.2 assumes a linear (diagonal) student vw(ε)=diag(w)ε, under which the result is essentially coordinate-wise ridge regression - it does not analyze the nonlinear students actually used, mode collapse/diversity loss, or the interaction between the distillation loss and the PDE penalty in realistic settings. Theorem B.1 concerns slow learning of a score coefficient in an idealized linear setting and does not directly establish that the Jensen's Gap is the dominant error source in practice.

Baseline fairness concerns: most baselines (ECI, DiffusionPDE, PIDM, D-Flow) are re-implementations in the authors' own codebase with weights chosen by the authors (e.g., ηt set to λtrain); PIDM and DiffusionPDE scoring markedly worse than the vanilla teacher in Table 1 is a red flag that baselines may be under-tuned. Hyperparameter transfer rules like λtrain=10^6 for stiff PDEs also suggest nontrivial per-dataset tuning despite claims of 'minimal hyperparameter tuning'.

Some reported numbers are hard to interpret or suspiciously favorable: PDE errors of order 10^-9 for Poisson/Helmholtz from a finite-difference residual on a 128x128 grid, and PIDDM-1 (one-step) nearly matching or exceeding a 100-step teacher on MMSE/SMSE/FPD, warrant stronger verification (error bars, multiple seeds - only variance in Table 12 partially addresses this).

Fidelity/diversity evaluation relies on FPD computed against a 'pre-trained PDE foundation model', which is not well characterized; the diversity analysis (SWD/APDD) is limited to Darcy. The paper's own experiments (Table 6) show distillation alone does not improve PDE satisfaction and the PIDDM advantage over the teacher is largely attributable to the added penalty and refinement loop, tempering the framing that distillation is the key idea.

Presentation and reference hygiene issues: duplicated references (Liu et al. 2023a/b are the same paper; LeVeque and Leveque 1992), a typo'd appendix heading ('Deviation' for 'Derivation'), an incorrectly stated Porous Medium Equation (u_t = ∇·(u^m ∇u) with a questionable closed-form 'exact solution'), and an oversubscribed related-work style that cites many image-inverse-problem methods with limited relevance.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the Jensen's Gap arising when PDE constraints are enforced on the posterior mean E[x0|xt] in diffusion training/sampling, with both empirical demonstrations (MoG and Stokes experiments, Fig. 2) and a supporting theoretical analysis in the appendix (Theorems B.1–B.2 on a low-rank Gaussian surrogate).

The proposed remedy is simple, practical, and well-positioned: post-hoc distillation with the PDE residual applied directly to the student's final output, decoupling physics enforcement from the diffusion trajectory. The method retains the teacher's versatility (forward, inverse, reconstruction) while enabling one-step generation.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: three main PDE benchmarks plus six more in the appendix (Table 5), a compute-matched comparison (Table 3), component attribution separating distillation from final-sample PDE supervision (Table 6), diversity preservation (Table 7), teacher-quality and architecture robustness (Tables 8–9), dynamic weighting for stiff PDEs (Table 10), and stability of latent optimization (Tables 11–12).

The evaluation protocol is fair-minded: the authors re-implement all baselines in a unified codebase, evaluate all methods on all three tasks, and openly note where one-step results only match rather than beat the teacher. The limitations section is honest (dependence on a well-trained teacher and reliable residual operator, residual tuning needs).

The framework is modular: ablations across distillation backbones (Rectified Flow, DMD, Consistency Model, Table 13) show the physics gain comes from final-sample supervision rather than a specific distillation choice, which strengthens the generality of the finding.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The core idea is essentially consistency-style distillation plus a PDE residual penalty on the final output. Final-sample physics enforcement already exists in D-Flow and noise-prompting methods (as the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix A.2), so the contribution is primarily a recombination of known components, and the paper's own framing ('simple yet effective post-hoc strategy') concedes this.

The headline efficiency claim is partially undercut by the results. PIDDM-1 (1 NFE) does not consistently dominate: on Darcy its MMSE (0.112) is slightly worse than the unconstrained teacher (0.108), and the best results everywhere are from PIDDM-ref, which uses 80 forward and 80 backward passes — i.e., the configuration that beats baselines is not actually one-step, and its refinement stage is conceptually close to the noise-optimization approaches criticized for cost. The efficiency advantage over ECI/DiffusionPDE at matched compute is real but less dramatic than the abstract implies.

Distributional fidelity is only empirically asserted. Penalizing the PDE residual on samples can systematically bias the student toward physics-plausible but distribution-distorted outputs (mode shrinkage), and the paper repeatedly notes that 'distributional fidelity claims remain empirical rather than an end-to-end theoretical guarantee.' The theoretical analysis covers only a linear diagonal Gaussian case with a linear student, far from the nonlinear PDE settings where the method is deployed.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance are reported for the main tables (Tables 1, 2, 5); only Table 12 reports variance for the latent-optimization stage. Given the small margins in some entries, reproducibility of the reported ordering is hard to judge.

Some baseline configurations may be under-tuned: e.g., DiffusionPDE's guidance weight ηt is simply set equal to the authors' λtrain, and the FM baseline in Table 5 is never defined in the text, raising fairness and clarity concerns. The main-text claim that 'PIDDM-1 already surpasses' posterior-mean methods is not uniformly supported (e.g., DiffusionPDE beats PIDDM-1 on Burgers MMSE/SMSE in Table 1).

Presentation issues: duplicated citations (Liu et al. 2023a/b are the same paper), a withdrawn submission cited (Dong et al. 2024), notation 'B' used for both batch size and boundary operator, and typos ('Deviation of Velocity Field' for 'Derivation'; 'FM' undefined). These do not undermine the science but reduce polish.
